414.title: The exile (2 Kings 25)
414.hook: Jerusalem falls in 587 BC and the Temple burns
414.howItsDone: Catholics hear the fall of Jerusalem in the Mass readings, pray Psalm 137 (136 in the Douay) on the Fourth Sunday of Lent in one year of the cycle, and the Church remembers the Holy Family's flight into Egypt when it speaks of care for migrants and refugees.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naaman, a proud general told to wash seven times in the Jordan. Your line was go and wash. What simple thing did you finally do? Day four hundred fourteen, and a new week.

Last week we stood inside Solomon's Temple as a cloud filled it. Today we watch it burn. The books of Kings have been warning about this for chapters: king after king turning away, prophet after prophet calling them back. Now the army of Babylon surrounds Jerusalem, under King Nebuchadnezzar, Nabuchodonosor in the Douay-Rheims. The siege drags on from the ninth year of the king into the eleventh. The food runs out. The text says it in one line: there was no bread for the people of the land. Then the walls are breached, in 587 BC by one common reckoning, and the last king of Judah runs for it in the night.
screen: `THE TEMPLE THAT WAS FILLED WITH CLOUD.` → `BABYLON SURROUNDS JERUSALEM.` → `NO BREAD IN THE CITY.`

segments.voice: Today's word is exile, and 2 Kings tells it with almost no comment, which makes it worse. King Zedekiah, Sedecias in the Douay, is caught near Jericho. His sons are killed in front of him, and then his eyes are put out, so that this is the last thing he sees. The next month the Babylonian commander arrives, and the Douay says simply: "he burnt the house of the Lord, and the king's house, and the houses of Jerusalem." The walls are pulled down. The people are marched off to Babylon, far to the east. Only the poorest are left behind to tend the vines and fields. Exile means more than moving. It means losing the land God promised, the king from David's line, and the Temple where God chose to dwell, all at once. Some scholars think much of the Hebrew Bible took its final shape in its shadow. This path has been here before. Back on day one hundred eighty-nine we sat with the psalm of the exiles, Psalm one thirty-six in the Douay: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." And the question they asked: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Today we've seen why they were weeping. But listen to how 2 Kings ends. Not with the fire. Decades later, a new king of Babylon lets David's descendant, Jehoiachin, out of prison, speaks kindly to him, and gives him a seat at his table for the rest of his life. A small, strange thread of hope. The line of David isn't finished.
screen: `THE LAST KING OF JUDAH, BLINDED.` · `THE HOUSE OF THE LORD BURNS.` · `UPON THE RIVERS OF BABYLON.` · `A SEAT AT THE KING'S TABLE.` · then, large: `HOW SHALL WE SING IN A STRANGE LAND?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for people who've lost their home. Settle, and breathe. Think of people who are, right now, far from the place they belong. Refugees crossing borders. Families whose houses burned or flooded. Someone sleeping in a car. Maybe someone in your own life who had to leave everything. Picture them sitting by strange waters, remembering home. If you pray, you can hold them before God, and ask for whatever they most need. If you don't, simply let yourself feel their loss for a moment, without looking away. The bell holds the time.
Exile. Being forced from your homeland; for Judah, the fall of Jerusalem, the burning of the Temple, and the long years in Babylon. Today's word.
Your line: by the waters again. Today, do one concrete thing for someone far from home: a donation, a welcome, a call to a friend who moved. Day four hundred fourteen.

screen: `DAY 414 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HERE AM I, SEND ME.`

415.title: Here am I, send me (Isaiah 6)
415.hook: Isaiah sees the Lord, the seraphs cry holy, and a coal touches his lips
415.howItsDone: At every Mass, Catholics sing or say the Sanctus, Holy, holy, holy, drawn from the seraphim's cry in Isaiah 6, and the call of Isaiah is often read at ordinations and on Sundays about vocation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the exile: Jerusalem burned, and the people wept by the waters of Babylon. Your line was by the waters again. Who far from home did you remember? Day four hundred fifteen.

Every Sunday at Mass, just before the Eucharistic Prayer, the whole church sings or says the Sanctus, the song that calls God holy three times over and says heaven and earth are full of his glory. Today we find where it comes from. We step back in time now, before the exile, to the prophets who warned it was coming. One of them is Isaiah, Isaias in the Douay-Rheims. And his book turns on a single moment in the Temple, in the year King Uzziah died, Ozias in the Douay, when a man looks up and sees more than he ever wanted to see.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY AT EVERY MASS.` → `BACK BEFORE THE EXILE.` → `THE YEAR KING UZZIAH DIED.`

segments.voice: In the Douay: "I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and elevated: and his train filled the temple." Just the hem of God's robe fills the whole building. Above him stand seraphim, a name usually taken to mean burning ones, each with six wings: two to cover the face, two to cover the feet, two to fly. And they call to each other: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." The doorposts shake. Smoke fills the house. And Isaiah's first reaction isn't wonder. It's terror. "Woe is me," he says, because I am a man of unclean lips, living among a people of unclean lips, and my eyes have seen the King. He's undone. Then one of the seraphim flies to him holding a live coal, taken with tongs from the altar, and touches his mouth with it: thy iniquities shall be taken away, and thy sin shall be cleansed. Not punishment. Cleansing. And only then does God speak, not to Isaiah but almost to himself: "Whom shall I send? and who shall go for us?" And the man who a moment ago said woe is me answers: "Lo, here am I, send me." In Hebrew, here am I is a single word, hineni. Abraham says it. Moses says it at the bush. The boy Samuel says it in the night. It means I'm present, I'm listening, use me. Catholics have kept this scene close. The seraphim's cry became the Sanctus at every Mass. And in the older form of the Mass, the priest prays before reading the Gospel that God would cleanse his lips as he cleansed the lips of Isaiah with a burning coal.
screen: `HIS TRAIN FILLED THE TEMPLE.` · `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `WOE IS ME: UNCLEAN LIPS.` · `A COAL FROM THE ALTAR.` · then, large: `LO, HERE AM I, SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say send me about one task. Settle, and breathe. Think of one thing that needs doing that nobody has volunteered for. At home, at work, in your parish or neighborhood. The dishes nobody claims. The hard phone call. The meal for the family that just had a baby. If something in you says woe is me, I'm not the right person, Isaiah said that too. Then, quietly, say his words about that one task: here am I, send me. If you pray, say them to God. The bell holds the time.
Here am I. In Hebrew, hineni: present, listening, ready. Isaiah's answer after the coal touched his lips: here am I, send me. Today's word.
Your line: here am I, send me. Today, volunteer for the one task you named, before anyone has to ask twice. Day four hundred fifteen.

416.title: A virgin shall conceive (Isaiah 7:14)
416.hook: the sign of a child named God with us, read by the Church as Christ
416.howItsDone: Catholics hear Isaiah 7:14 in Advent and on the feast of the Annunciation, and in the last days before Christmas the Church sings the O Antiphons at Evening Prayer, among them O Emmanuel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah in the Temple, a coal on his lips, answering here am I, send me. Your line was here am I, send me. What did you volunteer for? Day four hundred sixteen.

A king stands at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, outside his city, with an invasion coming. His name is Ahaz, Achaz in the Douay-Rheims, king of Judah, and two neighboring kings have joined forces against him. The text says his heart shook like the trees of the forest in the wind. Then Isaiah comes out to meet him there and says: be calm. Don't be afraid. Their plan will not stand. And he makes an extraordinary offer: ask the Lord for a sign. Any sign. As deep as the underworld or as high as the sky. And Ahaz says, very piously, no thanks.
screen: `A KING BY THE UPPER POOL.` → `HIS HEART SHOOK LIKE TREES.` → `ASK FOR ANY SIGN. HE WON'T.`

segments.voice: Ahaz says, in the Douay: "I will not ask, and I will not tempt the Lord." It sounds humble. Isaiah hears it as a refusal to trust. So he says: then the Lord himself will give you a sign. "Behold a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel." Today's word. Emmanuel, in Hebrew immanu El: with us is God. Here, it's a sign for a frightened king: before this child is old enough to know right from wrong, the two kings you fear will be gone. Now, the part where readers differ, and it's worth knowing who says what. The Hebrew word Isaiah uses is almah, usually translated young woman. Jewish readers understand the sign as a child born in Ahaz's own time. The ancient Greek translation, the Septuagint, renders the word parthenos, virgin. And when Matthew's Gospel tells of Jesus's birth, it quotes this verse from the Greek: "Behold a virgin shall be with child, and bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." The Catholic Church reads Isaiah's sign as finding its fullest meaning in Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, and Catholic tradition holds that a prophecy can speak to its own day and reach further at once. What everyone can see is the name. Not God far off. Not God above us. God with us, in the middle of a scared king's crisis, and, Christians believe, in a manger in Bethlehem.
screen: `I WILL NOT ASK.` · `IMMANU EL: WITH US IS GOD.` · `ALMAH, AND THEN PARTHENOS.` · `MATTHEW: GOD WITH US.` · then, large: `HIS NAME SHALL BE CALLED EMMANUEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say Emmanuel slowly. Settle, and breathe. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, say the first part, quietly: Emmanu. Breathe in again, and on the next breath out: El. Or say it in English: God, on the in-breath; with us, on the out-breath. Let it go slowly, like a heartbeat. If you pray, let it be a prayer: God with us, here, now. If you don't, let the words simply sit with you, and notice what it would mean not to be alone in whatever might be shaking you. The bell holds the time.
Emmanuel. Hebrew for God with us: the name of the child in Isaiah's sign, which Matthew's Gospel and the Church apply to Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: god with us. Today, at the moment you feel most alone, say the word Emmanuel once, under your breath. Day four hundred sixteen.

417.title: Swords into ploughshares (Isaiah 2:4)
417.hook: nations shall not learn war any more
417.howItsDone: Catholics hear Isaiah's vision of peace on the First Sunday of Advent in one year of the Lectionary, and the Church's teaching on peace, from Pacem in Terris onward, returns to it often.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sign for a frightened king: a child called Emmanuel. Your line was god with us. When did you say it under your breath? Day four hundred seventeen.

In the garden of the United Nations in New York there's a bronze statue of a muscular man swinging a hammer. In one hand he holds a sword, and he's bending its blade into the curved shape of a plough. It was a gift from the Soviet Union in 1959, at the height of the Cold War, which is its own kind of irony. And the idea it shows is about twenty-seven centuries old. It comes from the prophet Isaiah, from a vision so stubborn and so hopeful that both superpowers could stand in front of it and want it. Today's word is that vision.
screen: `A BRONZE MAN WITH A HAMMER.` → `A GIFT IN THE COLD WAR.` → `AN IDEA TWENTY-SEVEN CENTURIES OLD.`

segments.voice: Isaiah sees a day when the mountain of the Lord's house is lifted above every hill, and the nations stream to it. Not marched there. Streaming, the way rivers flow, except uphill. And the people say to each other: come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and he will teach us his ways. Then the line. In the Douay-Rheims: "they shall turn their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles: nation shall not lift up sword against nation." And the verse ends: "neither shall they be exercised any more to war." Most English speakers know that last line in another wording: they shall not learn war any more. Picture what that takes. A sword is iron. So is the blade of a plough. Same metal, reshaped. Isaiah doesn't imagine weapons vanishing. He imagines them being hammered, by hand, into tools that feed people. The energy that went into killing goes into harvest. And notice the order. First the nations come to learn God's ways. Then God settles their disputes. Then they beat their swords. Peace in this vision isn't just a ceasefire. It comes from learning a different way to live. The same words appear almost exactly in the prophet Micah. And the prophet Joel turns them inside out in a call to battle: beat your ploughshares into swords. The Bible knows both directions are possible. The Catholic Church opens Advent with this reading in one year of the cycle, and Pope John the Twenty-Third's letter Pacem in Terris, Peace on Earth, written in 1963, carried the same hope into the nuclear age.
screen: `THE NATIONS STREAM UPHILL.` · `SAME IRON, RESHAPED.` · `FIRST LEARN, THEN BEAT THE SWORDS.` · `JOEL TURNS IT INSIDE OUT.` · then, large: `NATION SHALL NOT LIFT UP SWORD AGAINST NATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end one small war in your life. Settle, and breathe. Everyone has one. A cold standoff with a sibling. A running argument at work. A comment thread you keep going back to. A grudge you've been sharpening for years. Name yours. Now picture the sword in your hands: the remark you keep ready, the silence you use as a weapon. And picture hammering it, slowly, into something useful. A question instead of an accusation. A first step instead of waiting for theirs. If you pray, you can ask for help to put it down. The bell holds the time.
Swords into ploughshares. Isaiah's vision of nations reshaping weapons into farm tools, because they have learned God's ways and will not learn war any more. Today's word.
Your line: ploughshares. Today, take one concrete step to end your small war: a message, a question, an apology, or just stopping the next jab. Day four hundred seventeen.

418.title: The wolf and the lamb (Isaiah 11:1–9)
418.hook: a shoot from Jesse's root; the Church draws its seven gifts of the Spirit from this chapter
418.howItsDone: Catholics are sealed with the gifts of the Holy Spirit in confirmation, many families keep a Jesse tree through Advent, and Isaiah 11 is read at Mass in Advent, including the Second Sunday of Advent in one year of the cycle.

segments.voice: Yesterday, swords hammered into farm tools, and nations that will not learn war any more. Your line was ploughshares. What small war did you start to end? Day four hundred eighteen.

A stump. Nothing left of the tree but a stump, low to the ground, the kind you'd trip over. Some readers see the royal family of David in it: once a great tree, now cut down. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of his root." A green shoot from a dead stump. Jesse was David's father, the man whose youngest son was out with the sheep. In Advent, some Catholic families hang ornaments on a Jesse tree, and this is the verse it grows from.
screen: `A STUMP, LOW TO THE GROUND.` → `A SHOOT FROM THE ROOT OF JESSE.` → `THE JESSE TREE IN ADVENT.`

segments.voice: Isaiah says what will rest on this new king. In the Douay: "the spirit of wisdom, and of understanding, the spirit of counsel, and of fortitude, the spirit of knowledge, and of godliness," and he shall be filled "with the spirit of the fear of the Lord." Count them: seven. And that's where the Church's list of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit comes from. Wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord. Readers of the Hebrew point out that it names only six: fear of the Lord appears twice. The Greek and Latin translators rendered the first one as godliness, or piety, and so the list became seven. Christians read the shoot from Jesse as Christ, on whom the Spirit rests completely. And the Catechism teaches that these same gifts are given to every Christian, sealed especially in confirmation, as steady dispositions that make a person ready to follow the Spirit's lead. Then the chapter's picture of what this king's reign looks like. "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb: and the leopard shall lie down with the kid," calf and lion together, "and a little child shall lead them." A toddler plays by a snake's hole and isn't hurt. Notice: the saying goes that the lion will lie down with the lamb. Isaiah actually pairs the wolf with the lamb, and the lion with the calf. Either way the point is the same. When the earth is full of the knowledge of the Lord, the old enemies stop hurting each other.
screen: `SEVEN SPIRITS ON THE SHOOT.` · `SIX IN HEBREW, SEVEN IN LATIN.` · `GIFTS SEALED IN CONFIRMATION.` · `THE WOLF SHALL DWELL WITH THE LAMB.` · then, large: `THE SPIRIT OF WISDOM, AND OF UNDERSTANDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for one gift of the Spirit. Settle, and breathe. Let the seven pass slowly through your mind: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety, fear of the Lord. See if one of them catches, one you could use this week. Counsel, for a decision. Fortitude, for something you dread. Understanding, for a person who baffles you. Choose it. If you pray, ask the Holy Spirit for that one gift, simply, by name. If you don't, hold the word and picture what your week would look like with more of it. The bell holds the time.
Gifts of the Holy Spirit. Seven: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord, drawn from Isaiah eleven. Today's word.
screen: `GIFTS OF THE HOLY SPIRIT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: wisdom, understanding, counsel. Today, when you hit the moment you need your chosen gift, stop and ask for it. Day four hundred eighteen.

419.title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40)
419.hook: speak to the heart of Jerusalem; they that hope in the Lord shall run and not be weary
419.howItsDone: Catholics hear Isaiah 40 in Advent, including the Second Sunday of Advent in one year of the cycle, and the voice crying in the wilderness is heard as John the Baptist preparing the way for Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and the seven gifts of the Spirit. Your line was wisdom, understanding, counsel. Which gift did you ask for? Day four hundred nineteen.

Handel's Messiah begins, after the overture, with a single tenor voice, almost alone, singing two words, and then singing them again: Comfort ye. Handel set the King James wording. But the words were written for people who needed them far more than a concert crowd. Five days ago on this path, Jerusalem burned and its people were marched to Babylon. Isaiah chapter forty sounds like a voice reaching those exiles, after years of silence by foreign rivers. And the very first thing God says is not a scolding.
screen: `A TENOR, ALMOST ALONE.` → `WORDS FOR EXILES.` → `NOT A SCOLDING.`

segments.voice: In the King James: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." The Douay-Rheims: "Be comforted, be comforted, my people." Said twice, the way you'd say it to a crying child. Then, in the Douay: "Speak ye to the heart of Jerusalem." Some readers hear in that Hebrew phrase a way of saying speak tenderly, the way someone speaks to win back a person they love. Her time of punishment is over. Her sin is forgiven. Then a voice cries out: prepare the way of the Lord in the desert, make a straight road. Every valley lifted up, every mountain made low. Christians know this voice: all four Gospels apply it to John the Baptist, getting the road ready for Jesus. Then a sobering line: all flesh is grass, and the flower fades, but the word of our God stands for ever. And then the image that ends the chapter. God, who never grows tired, gives strength to the weary. Young people stumble and fall. "But they that hope in the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall take wings as eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint." Notice the order: soar, run, walk. Not every day is a flying day. Sometimes the promise is simply to keep walking. Some scholars call these later chapters Second Isaiah and set them in the exile; the Church receives the whole book as Isaiah's, read as one. Jewish communities read this chapter on the Sabbath after their fast for the fallen Temple, and call that Sabbath Nachamu, comfort.
screen: `COMFORT YE, COMFORT YE.` · `SPEAK TO THE HEART OF JERUSALEM.` · `PREPARE THE WAY OF THE LORD.` · `SOAR, RUN, WALK.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL RUN AND NOT BE WEARY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: comfort someone today. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who's been in a long exile of their own. Grief that hasn't lifted. A diagnosis. Loneliness. A job search that keeps going nowhere. Don't plan a speech. Think about how to speak to their heart: one tender, simple sentence that says, it's not over, and you're not forgotten. Picture saying it, or writing it. If you pray, you can ask God to comfort them, twice, the way Isaiah says it. The bell holds the time.
Comfort ye. God's first words to his exiled people in Isaiah forty, said twice, tenderly: the end of punishment and the start of the road home. Today's word.
Your line: comfort, my people. Today, send your one tender sentence to the person you thought of. Day four hundred nineteen.

what it means: God's tender first word to exiles who'd lost everything: comfort, forgiveness, a road home, and strength to keep walking.
what a scholar hears: speak to the heart is a Hebrew idiom for wooing, speaking tenderly; and some scholars date chapters 40–55 to the exile, while the Church reads Isaiah as one book.

420.title: The suffering servant (Isaiah 53)
420.hook: despised, bruised for our sins, and by his bruises healed; read on Good Friday
420.howItsDone: On Good Friday, Catholics hear Isaiah 52:13–53:12 as the first reading of the Celebration of the Lord's Passion, before the Passion according to John and the veneration of the cross.

segments.voice: Yesterday, comfort ye, and the promise that the weary will walk and not faint. Your line was comfort, my people. Who did you send your tender sentence to? Day four hundred twenty, the end of week sixty.

A man is riding home in a chariot on a desert road, reading aloud from a scroll of Isaiah. He's an official of the queen of Ethiopia, a long way from home after worshiping in Jerusalem. That's in the Acts of the Apostles. A follower of Jesus named Philip runs up alongside and asks: do you understand what you're reading? And the man says: how can I, unless someone guides me? Then he asks the question readers still ask about this chapter: of whom is the prophet saying this? Of himself, or of someone else? The passage he was reading is today's word.

segments.voice: Isaiah's later chapters sing of a figure called the servant of the Lord, and in chapter fifty-three the servant suffers. The Douay-Rheims: "Despised, and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows, and acquainted with infirmity." People turned their faces from him and thought God had struck him. And then the voice in the poem realizes what was really happening: "he was wounded for our iniquities, he was bruised for our sins: the chastisement of our peace was upon him, and by his bruises we are healed." We thought he was being punished for his own wrongs. He was carrying ours. "All we like sheep have gone astray." And the servant doesn't fight back: like a lamb led to the slaughter, he opens not his mouth. Who is he? Readers have answered in different ways, and it's worth knowing who says what. Jewish tradition has often read the servant as the people of Israel, suffering among the nations, and some ancient Jewish readers saw a coming Messiah. Christians, from the earliest days Acts records, have read it as Jesus. In Acts, Philip begins from this very passage and tells the Ethiopian about Jesus, and the man asks to be baptized at the next stream. The Catholic Church reads Isaiah fifty-three every Good Friday, as the first reading before the Passion: the man of sorrows, the lamb who was silent, healing through wounds. And that's week sixty: exile, Isaiah's here am I, Emmanuel, ploughshares, the wolf and the lamb, comfort, and the servant who carried what wasn't his.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who suffers unjustly. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone carrying a weight they didn't earn. A child in a hard home. Someone wrongly accused. A person blamed for a family's troubles. Someone sick because of where they live. Picture them the way the poem pictures the servant: people looking away. Don't look away. Hold their face in your mind. If you pray, you can bring them before God, and ask that they be seen and healed. If you don't, simply refuse, for these minutes, to turn your face from them. The bell holds the time.
The suffering servant. Isaiah's figure who is despised, bears the sins of others, and by whose bruises we are healed; the Church reads him as Christ. Today's word.
Your line: by his bruises. Today, take one burden off someone who's carrying more than their share, even something small. Day four hundred twenty.

original.note: Hebrew: servant. Isaiah's servant songs center on the eved of the Lord.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prophecy about the crucifixion, written in advance.
what it means: a poem about a servant who is despised and silent, and whose suffering heals others. Christians read it as Christ; Jewish tradition often as Israel.
what a scholar hears: scholars count this as the fourth of Isaiah's servant songs, running from 52:13; Acts 8 shows Christians reading it of Jesus from the earliest days.
